newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl urged to raise human rights in Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: Kohl urged to raise human rights in Indonesia.

text.p: Nobel Peace Prize winner Jose Ramos-Horta on Friday called on German Chancellor Helmut Kohl to press Indonesian President Suharto to begin withdrawing troops from East Timor.

Speaking in an interview with German radio several hours before Kohl was set to depart for a three-day visit to Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan, Ramos-Horta said the trip could help democracy in Indonesia. But he said Kohl should not meet only government and business leaders.
"It is important that leaders like Chancellor Kohl...meet leaders of the opposition," Ramos-Horta said. "That would be an important signal to Indonesia.
"The visit could be very helpful for the situation in East Timor and democracy in Indonesia," he added.
Ramos-Horta, an exiled campaigner for human rights in East Timor, shared the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize award with the territory's Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo.
He urged Kohl to declare an arms embargo on Indonesia for a period of three to five years.

"It is very dangerous for Germany to introduce sophisticated defence weapons into the region. Germany knows very well that serious conflict could result when such weapons are introduced into regions where human rights are not respected."

Ramos-Horta, who lives in Australia, added: "How can Germany, that lost so many people itself during World War Two, sell weapons to a dictatorship like Indonesia, where people in East Timor have been killed with the weapons?"
Some 30 protesters met outside the chancellor's office in Bonn to demonstrate against German arms exports to Indonesia, and urged Kohl to hold a public meeting on human rights during his trip.
"He will perhaps talk about human rights in a harmless way, but that will have no effect whatsoever. He is not going to meet the Indonesian opposition," said Andrea Kolling.
"I think Kohl has a very big influence over Suharto," said Hok An, an Indonesian who has lived in Germany for 15 years.
"The German government is in practice the most important international supporter of Indonesia. Kohl promised to raise human rights, and I hope he will."
Kohl is taking 56 German industrialists to Jakarta with him.

Indonesia has been criticised for sending troops into East Timor in 1975 and annexing it the following year. The United Nations still recognises Portugal, the former colonial power, as the enclave's administrative authority.

A German government official said on Thursday Kohl would raise the issue of human rights. Even though Kohl did not have any plans to met opposition leaders himself, such contacts would be made by others in the delegation.
